response.content: Maps are never neutral records of the world; they are always political artefacts. Every map involves choices: what to include, what to omit, where to centre the image, and how to scale it. The Mercator projection, for instance, inflates Europe and North America while shrinking Africa and South America, subtly reinforcing hierarchies of global power. Borders themselves are contested claims drawn by governments, and depicting them in any particular way takes a side. Mapmakers must also decide which features deserve representation—roads but not poverty, rivers but not land ownership—embedding assumptions about what matters. Even naming is political: calling a place Burma or Myanmar, Persia or Iran, signals allegiance. Because no map can show everything, selection is inevitable, and selection always serves someone's interests. The map, therefore, is an argument disguised as a description.
